What it is

A free jukebox that shows you the music.

Aethra Kairos arrives already loaded — hundreds of original songs, free — and renders each one as live visuals driven by its real beat, key, and energy. Press play to start.

One artist

Every track is made by hand.

The whole catalog is the work of a single artist, and it keeps growing. Let the player build a set for you, or browse the library yourself.

It responds

You can steer it.

Drag to move the camera, pick a scene or a mood, tap the beat to lock the grid. The visuals, the mix, and the colour follow the song — and your input.

It fills the room

Every screen you own is one screen.

Say how many screens the room has and that many open — televisions, a projector, or little windows on this one laptop to rehearse with. They don't each play their own copy: they hold one field, cut between them, so a shape leaving one arrives on the next at the same height, the same size, the same instant. Move a window and the picture follows it — drag one onto the TV and its slice goes with it, live.

Measured, not guessed

It reads each track's real features.

Every song is analysed up front — its tempo, key, structure, and energy. That data drives the visuals and the DJ-style mixing between tracks. Opening it up for people to build on is on the roadmap.

Aethra Kairos

Every track here is by Aethra Kairos, and the visuals are drawn by the Möbius⁸ engine. It reads each song in real time — onsets, energy, and spectral shape — and cuts the scenes, palette, and camera to match. The geometry is mapped through a fixed function, φ(x) = 2·arctan x, so the look stays tied to the sound rather than to a random seed: amplitude and frequency place each frequency bin in space, with amber on one axis and ice on the other.

Milestones

Small marks for the first time you do each thing — kept in this browser, just for you.

Touch the visuals

The scene responds to your input: drag to steer the camera (the auto rig waits while you hold it), scroll to move closer or further, double-tap to send a shockwave through the scene. Your touch has a personality — and it performs it, in the music's own colours: the black hole wears a blazing photon ring with starlight shearing around the horizon; the vortex winds real spiral arms that keep spinning after you sling them; accretion is a disk of motes visibly orbiting and falling into your hold; ripples roll outward as true rings that crest brighter on the beat. Hold, and a thin arc fills as the touch banks power; let go and the charge detonates as a wavefront from the lift point — flick it loose for a bigger blast. The touch chip (or the immersive toggle) cycles the personality; AUTO lets each scene re-tune it. Two fingers at once plant two centres with opposite forces — a well against a void, two ripple sources interfering — and the metric bends the light through both. Every scene re-rolls its proportions each time it appears, and a five-act arc — OVERTURE · RISING · APEX · TURN · RESOLVE — follows each track from intro to outro, leaning the camera, the palette warmth, and the pace of the cuts toward where the song is.

And when you put the phone down, the field plays itself. After twenty-odd seconds of stillness a ghost hand starts working the same fabric your finger does — a ball bouncing off the walls, a snake turning on its lattice, a slow Lissajous curve, or short painted strokes with lifts between them; each room deals it a different one. It plays in phrases — a few seconds on, several off — never as hard as a real hand, softer still through an apex where the scenes are already doing the work, and sometimes it splits into a mirrored pair pulling opposite ways. The first touch takes the field straight back. Hold the touch chip (or press I) if you would rather it waited for you; it never plays for anyone who asked for reduced motion, or on ECO.

Everybody's hands

A second screen is not a monitor, it is a person holding one. So joining is something you do: type the four letters (or scan the code) and the field appears — then two questions, each answerable with one thumb in a dark room. Pick your colour, from eight that can be told apart across a venue and said out loud (“I'm the sea one”); it is yours for the night. Pick a look, from a tile per room drawn as the gesture of that room rather than a screenshot of it. What the room picks leans the director's deal toward those rooms — it never seizes it, so the night still belongs to the booth.

Then touch the picture. Your ripple appears on every screen in the room, in your colour, at the place in the wall you touched — so a hand on the phone by the window travels across the television behind the bar. That is the whole mechanic, and it explains itself the first time somebody else's ripple crosses your screen.

There is a game in it, barely. Touches that land near the beat push a meter that cannot be filled alone — it counts distinct screens, not touches, so drumming your own thumb does nothing and the only way up is other people. Fill it and the room answers: one bloom, in everyone's colours at once, across the whole wall. Then it resets. Nothing is scored, nobody is ranked, and the reward for playing is that the room looks better — which is also why everyone came. The bloom goes through the same flash governor as everything else here; a room that earned a moment must never be the thing that hurts somebody standing in it.

The dance engine

The visuals don't just flash on the beat — they move through it. Because the catalog carries a measured beat grid, the engine knows where the beat is, not just that it happened: a pull-back before the hit (anticipation), the impact, a damped rebound (follow-through), a lean into each bar, a slow rise across each 32-beat phrase, and a breath that never quite sits still. Even time itself is musical — the clock surges gently through each hit and relaxes between them. Staccato material moves sharp; legato material moves long. Paused, everything settles to breathing.

The room arranges itself

On AUTO the director is not shuffling scenes on a timer. It takes one reading of where the music stands — adrift · ascend · drive · apex · swarm · dissolve — and everything comes through that single word: which room is dealt next, how long it holds, which force answers your hand, how the field plays itself while you are not touching it, and how hot the colour runs. Four engines that used to roll their own dice now agree with each other, which is the difference between a show that arranges itself and one that shuffles.

Every room declares what it is for — the tunnel wants bass, the fern wants calm and no drum, the golden room wants coherence and no chaos — and the deal scores those appetites against the live music. It also remembers: the last few rooms are held back and let in again gradually, a room the night has not visited yet gets a lift, and the room you are already in is never dealt, so a change is always a change. Over a long set the whole gallery gets its turn instead of four favourites orbiting. A held-back passage is left to hold — the dwell stretches under the section's own intensity ceiling rather than cutting to a clock that cannot hear it.

The colour engine

The palette isn't random — it's read from the music. The track's detected key is mapped around the Camelot wheel to a root hue (the same mapping the Crate's key chips use, so the table and the room agree); minor keys sit darker and cooler, major keys warmer. The harmony scheme follows the music's character, and every scheme is a chord: the intervals of the key become angles on the colour wheel, so calm material reads as neighbours a semitone apart, quiet-but-restless material hangs on the fourth, driving energy earns the tritone, clean drive opens to the sixth, dense material settles into a triad, and material that is hot and arguing with itself aches on the seventh — which is a four-note chord, so it hands the gradient a fourth colour the three swatches cannot carry. Every change glides over eight beats of the measured grid in a perceptually uniform colour space, the way a lighting console cues, not the way a screensaver fades. Mix harmonically and the colours mix harmonically with you. The palette also warms through the arc — the same key runs hotter into an apex and cools again at the edges, as one rotation of the whole chord, so the intervals never move. The three dots in the HUD are the live palette — and they are also a button: click them to hold the room in SPECTRUM (a full wheel, anchored so the track's own key is the bright point the rainbow falls away from), DUOTONE (two colours, nothing pale to wash toward) or NOCTURNE (the chord taken down into the dark with a single light left in it), or leave it on AUTO and let the music choose.

Those three colours are stretched into a continuous gradient before any scene sees them, interpolated the long way round the colour wheel. A straight blend between two saturated hues is always greyest exactly halfway — which is where most of a spiral's arm or a coil's length happens to live — so the ramp walks the hue around instead and keeps chroma the whole way across.

And light no longer bleaches by accident. Hundreds of glowing sprites add up in the same pixel, and when a channel clips the colour dies before the brightness does: that white blob with a coloured rim is a hue failure, not a brightness one. Where the device can hold it, the field is now summed in high dynamic range and rolled off along a curve that compresses the brightest channel and carries the other two with it, so overdriven light reads as more saturated rather than as chalk (where it can't, each layer is held in gamut instead). Blowing out to white is still available — it is just a budget the music has to earn, opened by the act and the section's own intensity ceiling. A loud intro stays a colour. The drop gets the glare.

Following the music by eye

Bass, melody, and percussion each get a distinct visual voice, so you can follow the music by eye — nowhere more plainly than in PULSE, the visual meter: the bass is the ground, the melody is the ribbon, the percussion lands as ticks, and the bar itself is drawn as four circles with the downbeat heavier, so you can see the next hit coming. The HUD carries the same meter beside the scene dots. E nudges the field — a soft bloom, on request, for anyone steering without a hand on the pointer. CALM tightens the flash governor (a WCAG 2.3.1 luminance gate that is always on — no scene can strobe past it) and it engages automatically when the system asks for reduced motion, opening in PULSE, a room designed for that request rather than a dimmed copy of someone else's. FEEL, where the device supports it, taps the beat into the hand that holds the phone — the downbeat lands heavier there too.

The new wing

Scenes 9–13 came from the label's sketchbook. COMETS — neon meteor rain, every streak its own colour, speed riding the music's energy and the act. FERN — an iterated-function fractal drawn dot by dot as the track plays: sprouting through the overture, full-bloom at the apex, scattering to seeds at the resolve — each visit grows a different species. ROSETTE — spirograph rings drawn three times in offset channels, each one a different point on the live gradient; quiet converges them, every hit blooms the chromatic fringe. SLINKY — a chalk-grain coil whose spin direction is an argument you can win (drag sideways). OP-ART — a flat pattern machine that rolls between an isometric cube tessellation, a circular labyrinth around a black hole, an infinity-mirror dance floor lit on the grid, a scalloped psychedelic spiral, a dot-grid disco tunnel falling to its vanishing point, and dashed radar rings relayed in offset palette channels — joined now by four out of the demoscene's own book: plasma (four sines, the oldest trick there is), Chladni (the nodal figure of a vibrating plate, sweeping its modes the way a hand sweeps a signal generator), metaballs, and domain warping, where the stripes stay straight and the coordinate is what bends. All ten are closed-form arithmetic — no marching, no noise texture, no feedback buffer — and every one gets quantized into the same five hard colours with a dark seam between bands, which is what turns a wash into pattern. HALO — the spectrum bent into a ring: a torus of thousands of rainbow motes where each angle of the circle listens to one band of the live spectrum and swells where its band sings — an equalizer curled into a circle of light, threaded into bead-strands or relaxed into mist, with a beat soliton orbiting the ring.

The bench of lights

Scene 19 is FLAME — ten real light sources burning side by side: match, lighter, Bic, Zippo, Clipper, torch, campfire, an iPhone flashlight, an LED and a laser. Each one listens to its own band of the live spectrum and lifts when that band arrives, so the bench is a spectrum analyser made out of fire. Nothing in the room was art-directed. Every colour is integrated from Planck's law through the CIE 1931 observer: a Zippo is amber because 1500 K is amber, and the laser's green is a green no black body can make because 532 nm is one wavelength rather than a whole curve. Every flicker rate falls out of the flame's diameter through the Strouhal relation f ≈ 1.5·D−1/2, which is why the campfire breathes about twice a second and the match shivers about twenty times. The blue at the base of a Bic is CH* at 431 nm and the C2 Swan bands at 516 nm, summed beside the black body rather than blended with it, because light adds. And the orange at the tip is colder gas, not dimmer gas — the plume is a temperature profile before it is ever a colour. Your hand is a draught. The pointer is raycast into the bench's own plane and the plumes lean away from it, further the higher you look, because the base is tied to the wick and the tip is not; hold, and they are fed air and roar; let go, and the release blows them flat. A beam barely notices. A laser does not care at all — and that difference is the most honest thing in the room. Half the visits light the whole bench; the other half bring one source close enough to read the flicker off it. And then the bench fires. As the music earns it the room becomes a pyrotechnics show — gerbs and mines off the sources, shells that rise as comets and break at the top of their climb into peonies, chrysanthemums, willows, palms, rings, crossettes and strobes, with billows of lit smoke rolling out underneath all of it. It is the same two ideas taken a few thousand feet up. A star's colour is its chemistry, through the same observer: strontium's 650 nm red, barium at 515, copper's difficult blue at 452, sodium's D lines at 589, and a purple star that is copper and strontium in one pellet, so its colour is their sum. The gold willow is not a colour at all — it is charcoal, incandescing, and it comes out the same amber a Zippo does. And a star's flight is one closed form: linear drag on its velocity, gravity underneath, integrated once so thousands of them can live in a shader with no state. What separates a willow from a peony is not a different animation — it is three numbers.

The parlor

Scene 15 is PARLOR — the illusion machine. It rolls a century of perceptual science like dice: an Escher circle-limit tiling panned by true Möbius transforms, de Bruijn's five-wave Penrose skeleton, Carlson's multi-scale Truchet arcs, a sunflower's golden-angle swarm, moiré interference with its 57× leverage, the café wall shearing into the Fraser false spiral, and two of the oldest illusions on record — Hering's radial fan bowing two dead-straight verticals apart, and Zöllner's parallels splayed by alternating crosshatch — optionally garnished with Kitaoka's peripheral-drift ladder (the colours are static; your own eyes animate them) or the scintillating Hermann grid — plus a calculus-textbook vector field, one arrow per cell of graph paper, whose swirl tightens as the song builds. Every illusion is geometry, never strobe. And listen closely to what you see: several of these illusions have a measurable strength dial, and it rides the song's long-term energy — the picture lies harder as the music builds, and comes clean in the quiet.

The fractal field

Scene 7 is RIBBONS — six spectral ribbons that dissolve into mist as the music's entropy rises (double-tap the field to shatter them yourself). Scene 8 raymarches a distance field and rolls three ten-sided dice every time it comes up — form · surface · space, so the readout shows something like 4·7·2. Form (d10): BULB, QUARTZ, SPIRE (mandelbulbs opening at powers 8/4/3, then walking their dimensionality — eight beats standing on an integer rung, two beats morphing to the next, 3 through 9 and back, seam-free by construction), CUBE and VOID (mandelbox, positive and negative scale), SPONGE, TETRA, JULIA, OCTA, WEAVE. Surface (d10): orbit trap, shine and lighting — including DUO, which puts an amber π key against an ice e fill. Each surface routes the trap through a different pair of palette colours rather than spinning the hue, so the π/e identity survives every roll. Space (d10): kaleidoscopic MIRROR, orbiting ORBS, and TELE/WIDE lenses that compress or exaggerate perspective without changing how big the subject sits in frame. That's 1000 combinations, and the palette keeps rotating underneath them.

The lamp

Scene 18 is the LAVA LAMP, and the wax in it is not animated — it is simulated as a fluid. A couple of hundred particles, solved as a position-based fluid: incompressibility is a constraint the solver satisfies rather than a force it applies, so the wax holds a volume instead of a radius — which is why a pool spreads on the heater and a droplet is round without either being written down anywhere. Nothing decides that two blobs have merged, because there is nothing in the code that could: surface tension is a smooth pairwise pull, so two droplets drifting together are drawn the last little way by it, the contact widens on its own, and the neck fills in over about a second. A thread that thins past a point pinches, for the same reason and by the same number. Viscosity is the one line that separates wax from water — each particle takes a share of its neighbours' velocity — and at the amount this lamp runs, a blob struck by another does not bounce and does not ring: it deforms, and then it stops.

The rest is the thermodynamics, and they are the same as ever. Wax expands as it warms, so lift is temperature and nothing else. Cold wax is nine times thicker than hot wax (Arrhenius), which is why blobs go up briskly and come down like treacle. The clear fluid is one Rayleigh–Bénard convection cell written as a stream function — divergence-free by construction, so however hard the music drives it, it cannot leak. Two things ride on the same number the solver already computes: drag acts on the skin (a density deficit is exactly what "near the surface" means, and it is why a big blob rises faster than a small one), and heat enters through the skin too, then conducts inward — so a big blob has a hot skin and a cold core, which is the real mechanism behind the plume that lifts off the pool.

The picture is made the way real-time fluids are made: the wax's field is splatted — every particle draws its own kernel once into a small texture — so the cost of the surface stops depending on how many particles there are, and the fluid was allowed to get good. Four taps of that texture give the gradient, and out of it come an edge antialiased against the screen's pixels rather than the texture's, a real surface normal, and a thickness. The light is honest from there: refraction through that normal split into three wavelengths, over the coil's own glow in the liquid behind; Beer–Lambert absorption, so a thin edge is pale and a fat middle is deep; and the light that does not get through is exactly the light that comes back as the glow inside. The temperature is splatted alongside the density, so every pixel reads the temperature of the wax actually in front of it — a blob that has just left the coil is visibly hotter where it left.

Two details are doing more work than they look like. What gets splatted is not the density but a normalised field — each particle divided by its own density, which the solver already measured — because a droplet of four particles is genuinely thinner than the middle of a pool, and any threshold that draws the pool's edge correctly makes the droplet disappear entirely. The beaded chain of drops pinching off a rising column is on screen because of that one division. And one extra tap below each pixel gives the shadow: the only light in the object is under the column, so a blob is between the coil and everything above it, and without that the room reads as a flat cut-out however good the blob itself looks.

The music is the thermostat: bass and the act's own heat turn the coil up, and the rise, the stretch and the break-up all follow from that one number. Put a hand on it and the wax flows — and keeps flowing after you let go, because it has momentum — while the room behind the glass bends through the same metric every other scene answers a hand with. A device that cannot afford as many particles gets a coarser fluid, not a smaller lamp: the spacing and the kernel widen together, so the same wax fills the same bottle out of fewer, larger parcels.

Catalog

Put a catalog.json next to this file and it loads on start — that turns the page into a front-end for a hosted library (title, artist, album, genre, year, art, duration). Only src is required per track; the rest degrades gracefully. Sort by any column in the playlist. Shuffle plays every track once per pass before anything repeats.

Add your music — the label's loop

This site is its own record label, and publishing is a folder and one command. It runs on the studio machine, not on github.com — the analysis (beat grid, key, energy, the score the visuals dance to) happens locally before anything uploads.

One-time setup — open Terminal and run these two, in order (every command here is standalone: it works from any folder, any time):

git clone https://github.com/kmay89/aethrakairos.git ~/aethrakairos
brew install ffmpeg && python3 -m pip install numpy

(The second needs Homebrew; macOS already has python3 and git. pip's warnings about PATH or its own version are fine to ignore — the pipeline imports numpy, it never runs its scripts.) Formats: drop songs as they are. MP3, WAV, or M4A (AIFF and FLAC too) — anything that isn't MP3 becomes a 320k web MP3 on the way in, tags and the file's own dates carried over. No conversion homework; the public site still serves only web MP3s.

The loop — every time, forever. ① Open the inbox — the mkdir -p creates it if it isn't there yet, so this works on a fresh clone and in anyone's own fork:

mkdir -p ~/aethrakairos/masters && open ~/aethrakairos/masters

…and drag songs from the Music app into it. The folder is the album — the folder's name becomes the album's name, and a stale iTunes album tag can never override where you put a song. Loose files at the top level are singles: each becomes its own one-track release named after the song. The label's shelf today:

masters/ Echoes of Us Album I/ ← the three albums, one folder each Echoes of Us Album II/ Echoes of Us Album III/ Zenith.mp3 ← everything else sits loose = a single

Dragging out of Music copies the real files, and moving a song between folders later just re-files it — the publish date rides along. ② Publish:

cd ~/aethrakairos && ./publish.sh

It updates its own tools first (a quiet git pull — your inbox is never touched), then hashes, measures, renames, builds the catalog, runs the doctor, commits and pushes. A first pressing of a whole library takes a while — minutes of analysis, then a large first push; let it finish. The site updates about a minute after the push; the porch's Fresh pressing and the deck's pads pick the new tracks up on their own. Missing covers never block a release — the player draws a key-coloured monogram until you drop a cover.png into the album's folder. Want the once-over without publishing?

cd ~/aethrakairos && python3 make_catalog.py doctor

Re-drag your whole library any time — repeats cannot happen. Every file is hashed (an exact repeat is a no-op; a known file at a new path is treated as a move), and a perceptual fingerprint gate catches re-encodes. When a new file sounds identical to something already published under a different name, publish stops and asks which name wins: keep the existing, adopt the new file and name (the publish date survives), or keep both. Messy names tidy themselves — stray characters are cleaned, and two different songs can never claim the same public filename.

The dates are your story. Each track's publish date is read from the file itself — the day the song was made, carried through conversion — not the day it got dragged in. The playlist shelf's “The progression — first pressing to now” smart list plays the whole catalog oldest-first: the artist's arc, in order. masters/ is the inbox, ./publish.sh is the only button.

Notes

Audio never leaves this device. The interface fades while music plays — move the pointer to bring it back. The demo is Möbius Walking — a real Aethra Kairos track shipped beside the player and analysed by the same pipeline as the catalog, so the beat clock, the colour engine and the mixer all engage. Offline with a cold cache, a synthesized loop stands in — the engine still works with no files at all.

The player remembers

Queue, position, hearts, saved journeys and play history live in this browser only — nothing transmits, ever. On relaunch the player restores paused at the saved position: one tap resumes (phones require a gesture to start audio). On iPhone the music keeps playing with the screen locked; the visualizer goes dark in the pocket by design — playback never depends on it. Lock screen, Bluetooth, CarPlay's Now Playing screen and AirPlay all drive the same transport.

When a new version is published, an Update button appears in the top bar; applying it saves your place first, and everything (queue, position, hearts, history, journeys) comes back exactly as it was. Choose Later and that is remembered — the button keeps a small count of how many times you have put it off, stays quiet while the snooze holds, and reminds you once when it runs out. Nothing is ever applied out from under a set: ⚡ SHOW mode holds every update until you say so.

The Activity log, at the bottom of the Console, is the app's account of itself — updates offered and applied, what played, what the system decided, kept on this device and sent nowhere. If something ever feels off, that is the first place to look.
